An Arab citizen of Israel casts his ballot during Israel's elections in Umm al-Fahm, Israel, on October 27, 2026 [Amir Levy/Getty Images]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 28 Oct 202628 Oct 2026
Israel’s Arab parties are projected to win 18 seats in the Israeli parliament, exit polls indicate, after voting among Palestinian citizens of Israel surged to their highest levels in decades.
Exit polling data from Tuesday’s vote suggested that the leading Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, are set to hold a record number of seats in the 120-member Knesset. Updated exit polling indicated that the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party and the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party were tied at 51 seats each.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Israel heads to the polls as shift to the right dominates critical electionlist 2 of 3Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US electionslist 3 of 3Palestinian citizens of Israel can vote, but cannot expect changeend of list
Early indications put voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel at around 80 percent, historic numbers that break 1999 records, Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Tuesday.
The leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said he hopes the final election results will allow the anti-Netanyahu bloc, including his party, to win the 61 seats required to form a government.
“With the numbers we have now, there is no government,” Abbas told Israel’s Channel 12.
Abbas, whose Ra’am party currently holds five seats in the Knesset and joined the coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022, added that both main blocs reached out to his party before and after the election. ...

Supporters of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, react to the exit poll at his party headquarters in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 27, 2026 [Shir Torem/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 28 Oct 202628 Oct 2026
Israeli political leaders have traded sharp reactions to exit poll projections showing no clear winner between the country’s main political blocs.
Updated figures broadcast by Israel’s Channel 13 showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led coalition tied at 51 seats with the opposition bloc led by challenger Gadi Eisenkot in the 120-seat Knesset.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3No clear mandate projected in Israel election: What’s next?list 2 of 3A bad day for Ben-Gvir as he addresses his supporterslist 3 of 3Gaza’s women filmmakers turn pain into cinema as new academy launchesend of list
Despite narrower exit poll figures, opposition leaders insisted the result was a defeat for the government.
Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party and a former military chief of staff, told supporters after voting closed that the initial projections showed a “complete lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the October 7 government”, according to the AFP news agency.
“Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat,” opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement. “This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”
Under the updated figures, unaligned Arab parties were expected to hold 18 seats, leaving both major camps 10 seats short of the 61 required for an absolute majority.

Attendees at Gaza International Women's Film Festival [Eyad al-Qatrawi/Al Jazeera]By Eyad Al-QatrawiPublished On 27 Oct 202627 Oct 2026
Al-Bureij, Gaza Strip – A Sack of Flour, an 11-minute documentary by the emerging filmmaker Mona Abu Qass, draws on her personal experience to examine Israel’s use of starvation against Palestinians in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave.
The film is one of five documentaries by Palestinian women screened Monday at the opening of the second Gaza International Women’s Film Festival, which also marked the official launch of the Gaza Cinema Academy.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Do Palestinians in Gaza expect anything to change after Israel’s election?list 2 of 3Palestine weekly: West Bank under siege as Israelis go to the pollslist 3 of 3UN panel accuses Israel of ‘extermination’ in West Bank, genocide in Gazaend of list
The event took place at the site of the al-Nakheel Hall in al-Bureij, central Gaza, under the slogan “Women Creating Life from Death”. The hall is destroyed, like the majority of buildings in Gaza, after three years of Israel’s war, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
The film captures Palestinians’ struggle to find food in Gaza, the dangers at aid distribution points and the lives lost while trying to obtain flour.
Through Abu Qass’s own experiences, A Sack of Flour explores how the trauma of hunger continues to affect families even after food becomes available again.
Those experiences have renewed relevance as Israeli restrictions on goods entering Gaza and cuts to food assistance have caused shortages and fears of a return to famine.

Exit polls from Israel’s legislative elections have come in, with no party or bloc projected to secure a clear mandate to form a new government.
The polls, released by the major Israeli television networks on Tuesday, indicated that the coalition led by current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party was on track to win 51 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

The opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party was also projected to take 51 seats.
That could leave neither bloc with the 61 seats needed for a majority, setting the stage for weeks or months of political jockeying to form Israel’s next government.
Separately, the Arab-led parties, which are not part of either coalition, were projected to win 18 seats. This means the Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if other parties agree to join forces with them.
